articles.title: investingLive Americas FX news wrap 30 Oct: It’s a wrap: Nasdaq tumbles as AI costs worry investors; Fed speakers keep hikes in play
articles.desc: Nasdaq suffers worst month since March 2025 as technology stocks tumble Bitcoin tests key support as Binance security fears weigh Week ahead: Elections, rate decisions and jobs take center stage Earnings next week: Can Apple, Palantir and AMD restore confidence? Fed’s Logan: At least two more quarte
articles.content: Nasdaq suffers worst month since March 2025 as technology stocks tumble Bitcoin tests key support as Binance security fears weigh Week ahead: Elections, rate decisions and jobs take center stage Earnings next week: Can Apple, Palantir and AMD restore confidence? Fed’s Logan: At least two more quarter-point rate hikes needed Carney: Canada, EU working toward deepest possible partnership, short of accession Fed’s Daly: AI matters for near- and medium-term policy Fitch on UK Budget: Policy continuity leaves a tough delivery challenge Fed's Barkin: Direction of travel is straightforward for the Fed Canada GDP for August 0.0% vs 0.2% estimate US employment cost index for Q3 +0.8% vs +0.8% expected Morning Kickstart: Tech hammered as Amazon and Intel tumble; oil rises despite peace talk investingLive European session wrap: AI spending fears spook tech stocks; dollar falls alongside yields, gold October ended with investors taking a harder look at the cost of the AI boom. Technology led a broad stock-market decline as disappointing reactions to Amazon and Intel earnings reinforced concerns about spending, profitability and cash flow. Strong demand remains part of the story, but investors are becoming more demanding about when that demand translates into returns. The cross-market moves were revealing. Treasury yields declined even as several Fed officials argued for further tightening. Oil moved higher, keeping inflation concerns alive, while gold failed to benefit from lower yields. Bonds attracted defensive demand, but the protection did not extend across every traditional haven. Dollar finishes mixed after recovering earlier losses The dollar was mixed in the supplied late-session snapshot. Its strongest performance was against the euro, with EURUSD down 0.13% at 1.1164. Its weakest performance was against sterling, with GBPUSD up 0.11% at 1.3390. USDJPY slipped 0.06% to 157.59, while USDCHF rose 0.05% to 0.8246. USDCAD edged down 0.06% to 1.3979 despite disappointing Canadian growth data. AUDUSD gained 0.07% to 0.7032, while NZDUSD fell 0.07% to 0.5629. The mixed finish marked a recovery from the dollar’s broader weakness earlier in the session. Falling U.S. yields provided a headwind, but the currency market did not deliver a uniform risk-off response. Treasury yields fall despite calls for more tightening Treasury yields were lower across the curve in the supplied snapshot. The 2-year yield fell 6.43 basis points to 4.5917%, the 5-year declined 7.87 basis points to 4.7233%, the 10-year dropped 5.86 basis points to 4.9303%, and the 30-year eased 1.76 basis points to 5.3114%. The larger declines in shorter and intermediate maturities steepened the curve. The move was consistent with defensive demand as stocks weakened, even though the Fed commentary offered little reassurance that the tightening cycle was finished. Lower yields alone were insufficient to offset the concerns facing technology shares. U.S. stocks: Nasdaq leads the retreat The supplied end-of-day index readings showed: Dow industrial average: −573.08 points, or −1.09%, at 51,775.17. S&P 500: −140.32 points, or −1.82%, at 7,580.07. Nasdaq Composite: −747.73 points, or −2.86%, at 25,437.00. Russell 2000: −47.37 points, or −1.66%, at 2,811.84. Nasdaq 100: −1,017.66 points, or −3.46%, at 28,384.85. The selling extended beyond technology, but the Nasdaq indices carried the heaviest burden. The Dow held up better on a relative basis, although a decline of more than 570 points still reflected a difficult session. AI faces questions about financing and returns Amazon and Intel remained central to the earnings concerns. Investors questioned how much spending would be required to sustain AI growth and how quickly that investment would produce stronger profits and cash flow. A separate Financial Times report covered by InvestingLive added a financing concern: Blackstone reportedly told Anthropic that it might not obtain an investment-grade credit rating after its IPO. This was a reported possibility, rather than a ratings decision, but it sharpened the focus on borrowing costs. Intel was down more than 30% in that afternoon report, with substantial losses across chip and infrastructure suppliers including AMD, Arm, Marvell, Astera Labs and Coherent. Those were intraday readings. European stocks mostly lower European markets also finished mostly lower, with the UK holding a modest gain: Germany’s DAX: −221.47 points, or −0.85%, at 25,818.22. France’s CAC 40: −0.58 points, or −0.01%, at 7,969.43. UK’s FTSE 100: +7.73 points, or +0.07%, at 10,729.79. Spain’s IBEX: −204.70 points, or −1.09%, at 18,652.90. Italy’s FTSE MIB: −501.39 points, or −1.02%, at 49,290.91. Fed speak: More tightening remains on the table Today’s Fed commentary carried a predominantly hawkish message, although the speakers differed in how directly they addressed the next policy move. Barkin favored gradual adjustment, Musalem argued for another increase soon, and Logan outlined a minimum of two additional quarter-point hikes. Daly concentrated on AI’s implications for the Fed’s inflation and employment objectives. Richmond Fed President Barkin described the direction of policy as straightforward, with the pace still open to debate. He favored a gradual approach but pointed to resilient consumer spending, broad business cost pressures and companies preparing to pass those costs to customers. His comments on AI were particularly relevant to the day’s market debate: the investment surge is adding demand and straining supply chains, creating inflation pressures that monetary policy can lean against. His assessment suggested that economic resilience continues to give the Fed room to address persistent inflation. San Francisco Fed President Daly focused on how AI affects both price stability and employment. She emphasized that those effects matter for policy in the near and medium term. Her remarks did not establish a preference for a hike or a pause. The takeaway was that AI’s effects on the economy are already relevant to current monetary policy decisions. St. Louis Fed President Musalem delivered a more explicit call for action, saying rates would need to rise again soon. He viewed monetary policy and overall financial conditions as accommodative, with inflation unlikely to ease sufficiently without additional Fed action. Higher bond yields had tightened conditions, but not enough in his assessment. His preference was to act earlier in smaller increments, reducing the risk that delayed action eventually requires a sharper adjustment. A strong economy and labor market supported that approach, while inflation risks remained tilted higher. Dallas Fed President Logan was the most specific about the amount of tightening she considered necessary. She called for at least two more quarter-point increases to make policy modestly restrictive, followed by a pause to assess whether further action was needed. Skipping a meeting, in her view, would not change the destination. Gradual adjustments could help households, businesses and investors adapt, but she regarded the lack of progress toward the 2% inflation target as unacceptable. Her message made clear that a pause should not automatically be interpreted as the end of tightening. For traders, the distinction matters: Treasury yields fell on the day, but these remarks did not amount to a dovish shift from the Fed. Economic data: Labor costs moderate, growth signals soften The U.S. Employment Cost Index rose 0.8% in the third quarter, matching expectations and slowing from 0.9%. Wage growth eased to 0.7% from 0.9%, while benefit costs increased 0.9%, down from 1.0%. The report offered some reassurance on compensation pressures, although it did not resolve the broader inflation concerns raised by Fed officials. Chicago PMI fell to 55.3, below the 56.1 estimate and down from 58.8. Activity remained above the 50 dividing line, but the pace of expansion slowed. Canada’s August GDP was unchanged versus expectations for 0.2% growth. The advance estimate pointed to a 0.1% decline in September, reinforcing the picture of an economy struggling to build momentum. German preliminary inflation also came in softer than expected. Annual CPI and harmonized inflation both slowed to 2.8%, below forecasts of 3.0% and 3.1%, respectively. Oil rises as Middle East risks persist WTI crude traded at $102.89, up $0.89 or 0.87% in the supplied snapshot. InvestingLive’s oil coverage highlighted Houthi attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure and reports of U.S. preparations for potential strikes on Iran. Those developments kept supply risks in focus heading into the weekend. Elevated energy prices also complicated the inflation outlook, even as Treasury yields declined. Gold and silver join the selling Spot gold fell approximately $146.24, or 3.64%, to $3,874.33. Silver dropped $3.0644, or 5.88%, to $49.0756. Copper also declined 1.75% to $6.4870. Gold’s weakness stood out because Treasury yields were lower. That would normally provide support, but sellers retained control. InvestingLive’s gold analysis identified liquidation pressure associated with equity losses as a possible explanation: investors needing cash can sell liquid holdings such as gold to meet obligations elsewhere. That remains an interpretation of the selling, rather than a confirmed explanation for every transaction. Silver’s larger percentage decline, alongside weaker copper, also left the more industrially sensitive metals under pressure. Bitcoin remains under pressure Bitcoin traded at $76,803, down $989 or 1.27% in the supplied snapshot. The broader retreat from risk assets was compounded by concerns surrounding the reported Binance security breach. InvestingLive’s crypto coverage described exchange-security anxiety and leveraged liquidations as additional sources of pressure. Falling Treasury yields offered little relief as investors weighed both market-wide weakness and crypto-specific uncertainty. Next week: U.S. elections, jobs and central-bank decisions The November 2–6 calendar brings several important tests for markets, led by Tuesday’s U.S. midterm elections and Friday’s employment report. The results will help shape expectations for government policy, economic growth and the Fed’s next move. Monday starts with the U.S. ISM manufacturing report at 10:00 AM ET. Wednesday brings ADP employment at 8:15 AM ET and ISM services at 10:00 AM ET. Beyond the headline readings, traders will watch the employment and prices components for evidence of whether activity is slowing while inflation pressures persist. Tuesday’s midterm elections will determine control of the House and Senate, with implications for taxes, spending, regulation and the administration’s legislative agenda. The September JOLTS report, due at 10:00 AM ET, provides another measure of labor demand ahead of payrolls. Central banks also remain in focus. The Reserve Bank of Australia announces its decision Tuesday, November 3, Australian time—Monday evening in the U.S.—with several major banks expecting a 25-basis-point hike to 4.85%. The Bank of England follows Thursday with its rate decision and updated economic forecasts. Both events will test how policymakers balance inflation risks against the effects of tighter policy. Thursday brings U.S. jobless claims and preliminary third-quarter productivity and labor costs at 8:30 AM ET. Friday is the main economic event: U.S. payrolls, unemployment and average hourly earnings at 8:30 AM ET, alongside Canada’s employment report. Preliminary University of Michigan consumer sentiment follows at 10:00 AM ET, with inflation expectations another important barometer. Together, the reports will help determine whether the economy remains resilient enough to support further Fed tightening. What traders carry forward The next session begins with three connected questions: can technology shares stabilize, can Middle East risks ease enough to take pressure off oil, and will incoming data justify the additional tightening several Fed officials favor? Friday showed that lower Treasury yields alone are not enough to restore confidence when earnings, financing costs and inflation remain in question. This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

articles.title: Director Information reviews functioning of DICs across Kashmir division
articles.desc: SRINAGAR, OCTOBER 30: Director Information, Mamta Yadav today chaired a comprehensive review meeting to assess the functioning of District Information Centres (DICs) across Kashmir Division, with a focus on strengthening district-level information dissemination, improving media coordination and ensu
articles.content: SRINAGAR, OCTOBER 30: Director Information, Mamta Yadav today chaired a comprehensive review meeting to assess the functioning of District Information Centres (DICs) across Kashmir Division, with a focus on strengthening district-level information dissemination, improving media coordination and ensuring effective coverage of government activities and public welfare initiatives. Joint Director Information (Hqrs), Dr. Zahoor Ahmad Raina; Joint Director Information Kashmir, Syed Shahnawaz Bukhari; Deputy Director Information (PR/AV), Javid Ahmad Rather; Deputy Director (PR) Kashmir, Mohammad Rafiq Zullah; Deputy Director (Hqrs), Kashmir, Zubair Ahmad; Cultural Officer, Field Publicity Officer, District Information Officers of Kashmir division and other concerned officers also attended the meeting. During the meeting, the Director took a detailed assessment of the functioning of District Information Centres, reviewing their publicity activities, media outreach, field-level coverage, infrastructure, manpower requirements and overall performance. Stressing the importance of District Information Centres as the grassroots communication network of the DIPR, Mamta Yadav said that these centres have a significant role in ensuring that information about government policies, programmes, developmental initiatives and public welfare schemes reaches the people in a timely, accurate and accessible manner. "DICs are the face of the DIPR at the grassroots level. Their role goes beyond disseminating information; they serve as an important link between the administration, media and the public. It is imperative that every district unit functions with dedication, professionalism and a clear sense of responsibility," she said. The Director underscored the need to make publicity and information dissemination more dynamic, result-oriented and responsive to the changing media landscape. She called upon the district officers to effectively utilise digital and social media platforms alongside conventional modes of publicity to ensure wider outreach and greater public engagement. "Timely and credible information is the foundation of effective public communication. Our focus should be on taking verified information to the people through appropriate platforms, while ensuring that the achievements and initiatives of the Government receive adequate and factual coverage," Mamta Yadav remarked. She also stressed the importance of proactive media engagement and maintaining cordial and professional relations with local media organisations. She called for improved coordination with district administrations and concerned departments to ensure comprehensive coverage of important government events, public outreach programmes and developmental activities. Highlighting the need for innovation in departmental publicity, the Director encouraged the district units to explore local success stories, developmental milestones, cultural heritage and public-oriented initiatives for wider dissemination through print, electronic and digital media. "Every district has its own stories of development, innovation and public participation. Our officers must identify these stories and bring them to the forefront. Effective communication should not remain limited to official events but must also reflect the impact of government initiatives on the ground," she added. Mamta Yadav also called for greater accountability, regular monitoring and adherence to professional standards in the discharge of official responsibilities. She directed the concerned officers to maintain regular communication with headquarters, ensure timely submission of reports and strengthen the quality and consistency of departmental publicity. Reiterating her commitment towards strengthening the DIPR’s institutional capacity, Mamta Yadav said that a coordinated, responsive and technology-driven approach would be central to making departmental communication more effective and people-centric. She urged all district units to work with renewed commitment and ensure that the DIPR continues to serve as a reliable bridge between the Government and the people.

articles.title: AI Kickstarted A PHP Vulnerability Crisis. Can It Fix It?
articles.desc: CISA says hackers are actively exploiting two critical PHP vulnerabilities, prompting U.S. agencies to patch systems as experts warn AI is accelerating attacks and exposing outdated servers.
articles.content: AI Kickstarted A PHP Vulnerability Crisis. Can It Fix It? | IBTimes Last week, researchers at Google-owned Wiz, and Calif, an . The warnings about the vulnerabilities quickly spread online. Widely known as PHP2Shell, they enable attackers to take over targeted websites. , PHP runs across 70% of the web. As of this week, has confirmed that hackers are now actively exploiting a pair of critical security vulnerabilities in PHP and has ordered federal agencies within the U.S. government to fix their systems within the next three days. As organizations look to shut down affected services, the incident demonstrates how ill-prepared modern organizations are for an uptick in "For years, the technical difficulty of exploring certain software vulnerabilities offered organizations a safety net. AI is now showing that even the most complex vulnerabilities may not remain difficult to exploit for long," Arvind Nithrakashyap, cofounder and CTO at Rubrik told International Business Times. Amazon and Intel Plunge After Disappointing Results, Fueling Wall Street's Nerves About AI Spending America's Productivity Is Growing At Its Fastest Pace In Decades. AI May Not Be The Main Reason. "Patching quickly remains critical as the window to respond shrinks, but what patching doesn't tell you is whether attackers have already gotten in. With PHP2Shell, exploitation attempts were observed four days before patches were released, giving attackers an opportunity to establish access that could survive updates." Nithrakashyap went on to warn that organizations need to know exactly where they are exposed, including which systems and data could be at risk and whether attackers may have already gained access. He added that the possibility of compromise before a patch is deployed makes as important as prevention, as organizations can no longer rely on prevention alone. One of the issues with these vulnerabilities, which Cisco highlights, is that PHP 8.1 and older are end of life, whereas PHP 8.2 security support ends December 31 2026, with an estimated "The most dangerous assumption in the PHP2Shell incident is that the clock starts ticking when a vulnerability becomes public. Amazon recorded an exploitation attempt four days before the patch was released. Technical complexity can no longer be relied on to keep longstanding weaknesses out of an attacker's reach," Jay Bavisi, founder and group president of EC-Council told International Business Times via email. For Bavisi, it is a sign that patch management and incident response can no longer operate separately, with a need for teams to review historical activity for signs of exploitation. Roman Sannikov, global research coordinator iCOUNTER also noted the window between disclosure and exploitation is closing. "Attackers don't need a public proof of concept to start working. They now and build their target lists, so when technical details land, they are ready to exploit on day one," Sannikov said. Sannikov said defenders should treat today's patches as urgent and start with internet-facing systems, including the older PHP 4,5,7,8.0 and 8.1 sites that tend to be forgotten. In case, the high rate of PHP servers that are no longer reported, indicates many organizations are going to need to update their systems. From this perspective, AI may help defenders discover vulnerabilities faster, but it doesn't address systems that have been abandoned by the vendor , while attackers still have ample opportunity to surface potential exploits. © Copyright IBTimes 2026. articles.title: Patrick Stewart found 'Star Trek' fame but always returned to Shakespeare and the stage
articles.content: Patrick Stewart was a theater titan before 'Star Trek' brought him fame - WSB-TV Channel 2 - Atlanta Patrick Stewart found 'Star Trek' fame but always returned to Shakespeare and the stage LONDON — Before he captained the Starship Enterprise, And it was the stage to which he returned time and again, even after "Star Trek: The Next Generation" and "X-Men" made him The theater was where Stewart felt at home, and where he could fill an auditorium with his sonorous voice, tinged with a warm Yorkshire burr. Stewart spent a decade and a half with the Royal Shakespeare Company, whose former artistic director, Gregory Doran, remembered him as “a true Shakespearean” and “a theater actor in his bones.” In later life, he formed a memorable double act with his friend Ian McKellen, who called Stewart “the most respected and beloved actor of his generation.” London’s West End theaters plan to dim their lights next Tuesday evening in memory of Stewart, who died Wednesday in Los Angeles, aged 86. A passion for Shakespeare started in childhood He achieved both screen fame and stage kudos, a notoriously difficult balance. McKellen warned him against starring in sci-fi after Stewart was offered a role in which debuted in 1987. McKellen remembered telling him to "think of your stage career" rather than risk "getting lost in Hollywood for years and years." “Well, he took the risk and thank goodness for us all that he did,” McKellen said in a social media post after Stewart’s death. Across six decades, Stewart performed in plays by modern giants including Edward Albee, Arthur Miller, Samuel Beckett and Harold Pinter. But the work of William Shakespeare was his first love and his lodestar. During what he later called a “hand-to-mouth” childhood in northern England, Stewart’s love of theater was encouraged by an English teacher and by his mother Gladys, who performed in amateur dramatics. He memorized Shakespeare’s soliloquies for fun as a teenager, won a scholarship to the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School, then performed in rep, mounting a different play every week. It was an in-at-the-deep-end training ground for young actors that he said taught him: “Learn lines, hit your marks, don’t knock over the furniture.” Stewart was a core member of the Royal Shakespeare Company for a decade and a half from 1966, and later returned to the company, appearing in more than 40 productions. He moved from supporting parts to starring roles including Shylock, Prospero, Macbeth, Henry IV and Mark Antony. Doran recalled how, in a 2006 production of “Antony and Cleopatra,” Stewart had played the Egyptian queen’s consort as a military hero “no longer able to live up to his own PR.” “Patrick restored the magnificence of the role in a tragedy so often regarded as ‘her play,’” Doran said in a statement. He was a chilling Macbeth and a complex Claudius Stewart's starship captain, Jean-Luc Picard, had a ramrod-straight military bearing and an underlying humanity. In 2007, he combined a martial exterior with cunning and insecurity for Shakespeare’s “Macbeth.” In Rupert Goold’s production, set in a chilly dystopia, Stewart’s murderous Scottish ruler had what an Associated Press review called “pantherlike” magnetism, and a charged sexual chemistry with Kate Fleetwood’s Lady Macbeth. Stewart earned a Tony Award nomination when the show moved from London to New York in 2008. And he was in his element. “What I’m doing now is all I ever wanted to do,” he told the AP during the Broadway run. “I didn’t have any other ambitions.” Soon after, Stewart played Hamlet’s murderous uncle-turned-stepfather, Claudius, to David Tennant’s prince in an RSC production of Shakespeare’s tragedy. The combination of the “Star Trek” captain and “Doctor Who” star Tennant made the production a major draw. Hordes of fans thronged the stage door, and the RSC had to ban people bringing sci-fi memorabilia to be signed. But it was clear the casting was no gimmick. articles.title: Ireland joins European Lab for Learning and Intelligent Systems network
articles.desc: Alongside Norway, it is Ireland’s first time being included in the pan-European network.
articles.content: Ireland joins European Lab for Learning and Intelligent Systems network Ireland joins European Lab for Learning and Intelligent Systems network Alongside Norway, it is Ireland’s first time being included in the pan-European network. Ireland has joined the European Laboratory for Learning and Intelligent Systems (ELLIS) network after officially launching ELLIS Unit Ireland. The new unit marks the first time Ireland has joined the network, as ELLIS welcomed other new units in Austria, France, Germany and fellow first-timer Norway. The network has 49 units across Europe and aims to propel the continent as a leader at the forefront of AI research. The units operate as localised hubs whereby researchers can work together, share ideas across a range of disciplines and carry out long-term research. The unit is part of Rinn AI, which is Ireland’s national centre for research and innovation in data science and AI and is funded by Research Ireland. Prof Noel O’Connor, Rinn AI’s director, will lead ELLIS Unit Ireland, which will focus on advancing fundamental AI research in core machine learning and related areas such as computer vision, natural language processing and information retrieval. The unit will also work closely with domain experts, policymakers and societal stakeholders, as a means of addressing real-world challenges. There will be a focus on connecting researchers across the country and training the next generation of ML and AI researchers. Commenting on Ireland’s inclusion to the network, O’Connor said: “Joining ELLIS is a significant moment for AI research in Ireland. Through Rinn AI, we have brought together researchers from every university in the country and ELLIS Unit Ireland now connects that community directly to Europe’s leading network in machine learning. “It opens new doors for collaboration, gives our researchers and students a platform on the European stage and helps ensure the AI we develop is shaped by the people it serves.” , a photonics specialist in the School of Physics at University College Cork, about his plans for the semiconductors research centre that sits within Research Ireland’s new Rinn Network. articles.content: Grades from compulsory school determine which pupils are accepted into popular upper secondary programs. A new thesis from Uppsala University shows that pupils at for-profit independent schools have, on average, higher grades than would statistically be expected given their backgrounds. The findings suggest that grading is more generous in independent schools and that the differences in grades may give pupils from high-income households a greater advantage in the competition for places at upper secondary school, at the expense of other pupils.

articles.title: Scientists have reconstructed the face of a human from 315,000 years ago and it looks very familiar
articles.desc: Scientists have reconstructed the face of the oldest known Homo sapiens from 315,000 years ago, found at Jebel Irhoud, Morocco.
articles.content: Oldest Homo sapiens face from Morocco looks familiar Scientists have reconstructed the face of a human from 315,000 years ago and it looks very familiar Scientists have digitally reconstructed the face of the oldest known and the result is not what most people would expect from someone who lived 315,000 years ago. He looks like a person you might walk past on the street. The face, built from fossil fragments found in a Moroccan mine in the 1960s, has heavy brows, a broad nose, and a projecting jaw. He looks strong. He looks weathered. But he does not look alien. He does not look like a textbook illustration of a 'caveman'. He looks, give or take a few structural details, like someone who could be sitting across from you on the subway. "As for the individual from Jebel Irhoud, he might go unnoticed in a crowd," said 3D designer Cícero Moraes, who led the reconstruction. "But a closer look would reveal something that sets him apart from the rest - most notably his robust features and a projecting jaw." The fossils were found at Jebel Irhoud, a mining site in western Morocco. A worker extracting minerals in the early 1960s discovered a skull. initially thought it belonged to an African Neanderthal from roughly 40,000 years ago. Later excavations uncovered more human remains and stone tools. In 2017, two landmark studies identified the remains as early members of our own species, Homo sapiens, and dated the fossil-bearing layer to approximately 315,000 years old. That pushed the known history of our species back by around 100,000 years. These were the oldest Homo sapiens fossils ever found. And now they have a face. A fascinating glimpse into the past. Credit: Cicero Moraes There was no complete skull from a single individual to work with. Scientists at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology had previously combined different fossil specimens found in the same archaeological layer into a digital composite skull. Most of the braincase and upper face came from the original skull, known as Irhoud 1. The lower jaw and teeth came from another individual found at the same site. Moraes and his team started from images and video of the composite skull released alongside the 2017 research. They extracted frames and used overlapping views to calculate a three-dimensional model, checking its scale against published measurements. To estimate the soft tissue covering the bones, they used a CT scan of a modern adult and digitally reshaped the donor's skull to match the ancient model. The facial tissue changed with it, providing a starting point. Measurements of tissue thickness from living people were used to refine the result. The team checked the skull model's internal dimensions. Its cranial cavity measured 1,364 millilitres, close to an earlier estimate of 1,375 millilitres calculated from CT scans of the actual fossil. That agreement supports the model's proportions, though it cannot prove that the face is accurate because no soft tissue survives from 315,000 years ago to compare it against. The 2017 analysis of the fossils identified something that had not been expected. The Jebel Irhoud individuals had modern-looking faces but archaic-looking braincases, suggesting that the features we associate with present-day humans did not all evolve at the same time. The face came first. The rounded skull shape we have now developed later. That is visible in the reconstruction. From the front, the face reads as human. The eyes, the nose, the proportions of the mouth all look familiar. From the side, the skull is slightly elongated compared to a modern human, a reminder that this is not someone from the 21st century no matter how recognisable he appears head-on. The coloured version of the reconstruction, which includes skin pigmentation, hair, and a beard, is described by Moraes as 'the most artistic version' and the one containing 'fewer scientifically robust features'.
